summary: The agent (Codex/gpt-6.1-sol) investigated the dispatch tool, identified several real bugs (gas billing conversion, missing part-load points, LT radiator heat misuse, missing startup costs, UTC/local time misalignment) and rewrote dispatch.py/planner to fix them, finishing in about 13 minutes against an 8-hour budget. Its fix produces a correct, deterministic plan for the single visible day supplied in its sandbox (all visible test assertions pass), but it had no access to the four hidden evaluation days (h1-h4) or to tests/solution directories. When the fixed tool is actually run against the hidden days, it crashes with 'RuntimeError: no feasible loading' (e.g. at 00:00 for h1, where both engines GE1 and GE2 are running simultaneously at midnight, a configuration not present in the visible day's status.json). This caused all hidden-day tests to error out and the overall reward to be 0.0 despite the visible-day tests passing cleanly. The failure is concentrated in exactly the kind of plant/physical-modeling logic (multi-engine combinations, maintenance-outage interactions) that the task author identifies as the intended core difficulty, rather than in an unrelated bug, infrastructure issue, or policy refusal.

task_specification.explanation: instruction.md (confirmed as the full, short file) directs the agent to the data files (plant.json, supply.json, status.json, demand.csv, weather.csv) which encode the physical model the agent must reason about, and explicitly states the plan must keep its existing format with every figure consistent with how the plant runs. The task's own difficulty_explanation in README.md states that diagnosing physical-modelling errors (heat-circuit routing, maintenance dependencies, absorption-chiller cooling-water requirements) 'requires plant knowledge to identify' and is 'part of an energy centre operations engineer's work' -- i.e. the implicit domain-knowledge burden is an intentional feature of the task, not a specification gap. The verifier's reference.py recomputes every balance/limit from the plan's own unit outputs rather than relying on undocumented exact-match strings, so there is no hidden hardcoded format the instructions failed to disclose. The agent's failure traces to genuinely difficult multi-engine/maintenance interaction logic, not to missing or ambiguous instructions.

reward_hacking.explanation: The agent's trajectory shows it only reading/editing /app/dispatch.py and /app/planner and testing against /app/data (the single visible day baked into its own container, per environment/Dockerfile which only COPYs data/planner/dispatch.py). The artifacts manifest confirms only dispatch.py and planner/ were produced as artifacts; the agent's sandbox never had access to /app/task/tests, /app/task/solution, or the hidden day fixtures, so it could not have copied from the solution or crafted answers to specific hidden tests. There is no evidence in the trajectory of writing to /logs/verifier/reward.txt, modifying test files, or any other manipulation of the grading mechanism -- the final message describes legitimate debugging and a self-reported regression suite ('All 13 regression tests pass') that the agent wrote itself.

difficulty_crux.explanation: task.toml's README.md difficulty_explanation states the core challenge is physical-modelling correctness: engine heat-circuit routing with no dump radiator, maintenance on heat-circuit components taking out dependent plant, and absorption-chiller cooling-water requirements, needing correct handling across varied outage/weather scenarios. Running the agent's actual fixed dispatch.py against the hidden fixtures reproduces 'RuntimeError: no feasible loading at 00:00' for h1, h2, h4 (and 13:30 for h3) -- h1's status.json has both GE1 and GE2 running simultaneously at midnight (unlike the visible day, which only had GE1 running at midnight with a different outage pattern), indicating the agent's engine-combination/part-load or maintenance-outage logic still has a feasibility bug that only manifests under plant configurations not exercised by the single visible day. This is squarely the class of plant-physics/maintenance-interaction bug the author calls out as the intended difficulty, not an unrelated environment or formatting issue.

near_miss.explanation: The run is not a narrow miss: 4 of the 5 evaluated days (h1, h2, h3, h4) crash outright with an unhandled RuntimeError before any plan is produced, which test_plans.py treats as 'no plan' (errors, not close numeric misses) -- 40 test errors plus 4 explicit 'test_same_plan_every_time' failures, against only 11 passes, all on the single visible day. Since the hidden days fail by producing no output at all rather than a plan that is quantitatively close to a cost/tolerance threshold, this is a wide-margin, structural failure (the optimizer could not even complete) rather than a solution that just missed a tight numeric bound.

refusals.explanation: The trajectory shows the agent engaging fully with the task from step 6 onward, narrating specific bug diagnoses (gas billing direction, missing part-load points, LT radiator heat, startup costs, UTC/local time misalignment, heat-circuit outages) and producing a final deliverable with a cost/gas/starts summary. There is no refusal language, no citation of content/safety policy, and no early abort -- the agent worked for the full ~13 minutes of its active session and delivered a completed (if ultimately buggy) fix.

low_timeout.explanation: agent_execution started at 2026-10-20T06:15:24.702Z and finished at 2026-10-20T06:27:43.835Z, roughly 12 minutes 19 seconds elapsed, against an allotted agent timeout_sec of 28800 (8 hours) per task.toml. The agent explicitly concluded with a final summary message declaring the fix complete and regression tests passing, rather than being cut off mid-edit or mid-command. There is no evidence of the agent still working, looping, or making incremental progress near a timeout boundary -- it stopped voluntarily, far short of the time budget, having (incorrectly) judged the fix complete.
